reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Burn depth is classified as superficial (epidermal), superficial and deep partial thickness (dermal), and full thickness, with depth guiding whether a wound will heal spontaneously or require excision and grafting

Extent of burn is estimated using the rule of nines, Lund-Browder charts, or the patient's palm as roughly one percent of body surface area, and only partial and full thickness areas are counted for resuscitation
Fluid resuscitation for major burns is guided by a weight and burn-area formula (Parkland formula) with crystalloid titrated to urine output rather than to a fixed volume
Deep circumferential burns of a limb or the torso can produce a tourniquet or restrictive effect, and escharotomy may be needed to restore perfusion or ventilation
Early wound care emphasises cleaning, appropriate dressings, and preventing infection, while deep dermal and full thickness wounds benefit from early tangential excision and skin grafting
Inhalation injury, facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the airway, and hoarseness signal potential airway compromise that can progress rapidly to obstruction
Adequate analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, nutritional support, and prevention of hypothermia are integral to burn care
Referral to a specialist burn centre is indicated for large burns, burns of the face, hands, feet, perineum or major joints, electrical and chemical burns, and burns with inhalation injury
reference.pathophysiology: A burn causes coagulative tissue necrosis whose severity depends on temperature and contact time. Jackson described three zones: a central zone of coagulation (irreversible necrosis), a surrounding zone of stasis with compromised perfusion that can be salvaged or progress to necrosis, and an outer zone of hyperaemia. Large burns trigger a systemic inflammatory response with release of mediators that increase capillary permeability, causing fluid shift from the intravascular space into the interstitium and burn oedema. This produces hypovolaemia (burn shock) and, if inadequately treated, organ hypoperfusion. Loss of the skin barrier impairs thermoregulation and fluid balance and predisposes to infection and hypermetabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Non-accidental injury in children with suspicious patterns
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of burn depth and total body surface area using Lund-Browder chart
Carboxyhaemoglobin level and arterial blood gases when inhalation injury or carbon monoxide exposure is suspected
Bronchoscopy to assess airway and inhalation injury
Baseline and serial electrolytes, renal function, and haematocrit to guide resuscitation
ECG and cardiac monitoring after high-voltage electrical injury
Creatine kinase and urine myoglobin when deep or electrical injury raises concern for rhabdomyolysis
redFlags: Signs of inhalation injury or impending airway obstruction (facial burns, stridor, hoarseness, soot in the airway) requiring early intubation
Large burns causing burn shock and needing prompt fluid resuscitation and burn centre transfer
Circumferential deep burns of a limb or the chest threatening perfusion or ventilation and requiring escharotomy
High-voltage electrical injury with cardiac arrhythmia or rhabdomyolysis
Features of burn wound sepsis or necrotising infection
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on burn size and depth, age, inhalation injury, and comorbidity. Superficial and superficial partial thickness burns generally heal without surgery and with minimal scarring, whereas deep dermal and full thickness burns require grafting and are prone to hypertrophic scarring and contracture. Timely resuscitation, early excision, infection control, and rehabilitation markedly improve survival and functional recovery.
pitfalls: Overestimating or underestimating burn size, leading to inappropriate fluid resuscitation and either oedema or under-resuscitation
Counting superficial erythema when calculating burn area for resuscitation
Delaying recognition of inhalation injury until airway swelling makes intubation difficult
Failing to reassess deep dermal burns, which may convert to full thickness and need grafting
Neglecting hypothermia, analgesia, and nutrition during the acute phase
Missing the need for escharotomy in circumferential deep burns
